reasoning.Student A:
The key property says the set of schools you can possibly be matched with (the Obtainable Schools) is fixed regardless of how you rank them. Your submitted ranking only chooses which school you get among that fixed set — you receive the highest-ranked school (in your submitted list) that lies in the Obtainable Schools. Therefore you cannot use your ranking to expand or shift the attainable set; the only sensible goal is to ensure that, whatever the obtainable set turns out to be, the school you most prefer among those is listed highest.

Given that, the optimal strategy is to rank sincerely according to your true preferences: put y first (you prefer y most and have priority 1 there), then x, then z, then w. This guarantees that if y is obtainable you get it; if not but x is obtainable you get x; and so on. Trying to manipulate the order cannot make an unreachable school obtainable.
reasoning.Student B:
Because the mechanism guarantees that the set of schools I could possibly be matched with (my Obtainable Schools) is fixed given the other students' rankings and schools' priorities, my submitted ranking cannot change which schools are obtainable for me. The ranking only selects which school I get within that fixed set: I will receive the highest-ranked school among my Obtainable Schools.

Given that, the dominant strategy to maximize my outcome is to rank the schools in my true preference order (y > x > w > z). Putting any less-preferred school above a more-preferred one cannot broaden my Obtainable Schools and only risks giving me a worse assignment if both are obtainable. My priority strengths (priority 1 at x and z, priority 2 at y and w) and the fact that most others also prefer y > x > w > z may affect which schools are actually in my Obtainable set, but they do not change the fact that I should rank honestly to ensure I get the best available school from that fixed set.

Because the mechanism fixes the set of schools I could possibly receive (my Obtainable Schools) regardless of how I rank them, my ranking cannot change which schools are obtainable — it only selects the most-preferred school among that fixed set. Therefore the dominant strategy is to list my true preferences so that, once the mechanism chooses among the obtainable schools, I get the best one for me.

Given my true tastes (y > x > z > w) and the priorities, I should rank schools in that true order. The fact that most applicants favor y > x > w > z and that my priorities at y and z are lower doesn't change this conclusion: it may affect which schools are in my obtainable set, but it is not something I can influence by misranking. So I report my genuine preference order.
